# Helping your midwife find you

**Riverside Community Midwives – Home Birth Welcome Pack**

Hello, and welcome. This page comes from all of us at Riverside, but I’m the one who keeps getting lost, so I’ve been given the job of writing it.

Some of you are having your first baby. Some have done this before. Either way, there’s a lot to remember, and the practical things are easy to forget. This isn’t a list of rules and nobody is going to tell you off. It’s just the stuff that helps us get to you quickly — especially at 3am when baby is coming and we’re carrying half the equipment we own.

## First, the 37 week bit

Home birth cover starts from **37 weeks**.

Before 37 weeks, if labour starts, you go to the hospital. We tell everyone this at booking, but it’s a lot to take in, and people forget. That’s normal. Put it in your phone, tell your birth partner, and write it on the fridge checklist at the end.

If labour starts before 37 weeks, phone the hospital maternity unit. If you are 37 weeks or more and think labour is starting, phone the Riverside birth line.

If you’re not sure whether it’s labour, you can still ring the birth line once you’re 37 weeks. We’d rather talk it through with you than have you sitting at home worrying.

## Calling us when labour starts

When labour starts, phone the **Riverside birth line**.

The number should be in your notes and on the fridge checklist. The birth line goes to whoever is on call, so you get the right midwife.

Please don’t phone or text my personal mobile first — even if I’ve given you the number and even if I’m lovely. I might be off duty, asleep, at another birth, or in the middle of something. The birth line is the proper way to reach the midwife who is on call.

Save the number now. Not at 3am when you’re breathing through a contraction and trying to find your glasses.

## Help us find your front door

Make sure your house number or name is easy to see. If you live in a flat, tell us the building name, the block, the floor, and which entrance. If your house has a name instead of a number, please tell us clearly.

One of us once tried to find “Rosemary Cottage” in a street of terraces and the sat nav took her to a chippy. True story. Lovely chips, wrong house.

If your address is tricky, you can send a pin on WhatsApp to the **birth line phone**, or use what3words. The what3words app is actually really good. Please send it to the birth line phone, not my personal mobile.

At night, please put the porch light on. Dark streets in winter all look the same, and we are not vampires — we just need to see the door.

If you want to put balloons on the gate like it’s a party, please do. One family did that and it was the best idea ever. We found them straight away. A simple sign works too.

And if you see a midwife peering through your window, it might be me. I once walked into the wrong house because the door was open. A lovely old man gave me a Jammie Dodger anyway. He was very kind. He was not the right house.

## Parking

Two midwives come to a home birth, usually in separate cars. If possible, please keep two parking spaces free. We know that’s not always possible, especially in some streets, but it helps a lot.

If you live in a permit zone around Anfield or Kensington, ask the council about a visitor permit, or have one ready on the dashboard. We’ve had parking tickets before. Nobody wants to be sorting out a ticket while someone is in labour.

## What we’re carrying

We bring a lot with us: gas and air cylinders, the big bag, and sometimes birthing pool stuff. Our arms get tired.

So if you can, keep a clear path from the street to your door, and keep the stairs and hallway clear. We’re not coming to inspect your house. We don’t care about dust. We do care about being able to get in safely and move around without tripping.

Please clear the stairs and hallway — no shoes, no washing basket, no Lego. Especially Lego. Lego at 3am is its own kind of birth emergency.

## Pets

We love pets. I really do love dogs. I once looked after a staffie called Pippin who loved me too much. She jumped up at me every visit and I nearly dropped the gas and air. She was gorgeous.

But during the birth, please put pets in another room with someone they know. Not because they’re bad, and not because we don’t like them. It’s just that we need space, you need calm, and nobody needs a dog trying to help with the Entonox.

## People in the house

If you have family or friends with you, it helps if one person can be on door duty — watching for us, keeping the phone close, and keeping pets out of the way. Not a rule, just handy.

## One last thing

This isn’t about having a perfect house. It’s about helping us get to you and do our job. If you haven’t done any of it, we still want to come. We’re not going to stand on the step ticking boxes.

In the Philippines we say the midwife is like family. That’s how I feel about the families I look after. We’re coming as a friend — a friend with a lot of bags and a torch, but a friend.

If you’re worried about anything on this page, ask us at your next appointment. We’d rather talk it through now than have you worrying.

And if 3am arrives and your hallway is full of Lego and the dog is on the sofa, don’t panic. Phone us. We’ll find you. Eventually. But please put the porch light on.

---

# Fridge checklist

Tick what you’ve done. Stick this on the fridge. No pressure — it’s just to help.

☐ I have saved the **Riverside birth line** number in my phone.

☐ I know home birth cover starts at **37 weeks**.

☐ I know that before 37 weeks, I phone the hospital maternity unit, not the home birth line.

☐ My birth partner knows to phone the **birth line**, not my midwife’s personal mobile.

☐ My house number or name is easy to see from the street.

☐ I have written down any flat, block, floor, or entrance details.

☐ If my address is tricky, I have sent a WhatsApp pin or what3words to the birth line phone.

☐ My porch light works, and I can put it on at night.

☐ I have thought about parking, and whether I need a visitor permit.

☐ I have cleared a path to the door and kept the stairs and hallway clear.

☐ I have a plan for pets to go in another room with someone they know.

☐ I have a sign, balloons, or something visible if my house is hard to find.

☐ I know two midwives usually come, in separate cars, with a lot of equipment.

☐ I know I can ring the birth line if I’m not sure whether labour is starting, once I’m 37 weeks.

**Riverside Community Midwives**  
*We’re coming as friends. We just need to find the door.*
